meta.description: This Job Safety Training Outline (JSTO) establishes the occupational safety requirements for personnel assigned to the Avionics and Electrical & Environmental (E&E) Maintenance work centers. While a portion of their workload involves low-risk, precision bench-level testing and system programming within controlled hangar shops, personnel are routinely required to operate on active flightlines and in heavy maintenance bays. During these on-aircraft operations, technicians are directly exposed to severe industrial hazards, including high-voltage electrical circuits, high-intensity Radio Frequency Radiation (RFR), extreme flightline noise, jet engine intake/exhaust, and moving ground equipment. Consequently, personnel in these work centers require comprehensive hazard recognition training and must be proficient in the use of specialized Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) to safely navigate active flightlines and execute live aircraft electronics maintenance.

meta.fireEquipmentNotes:
EMERGENCY EYE WASH/SHOWERS: No corrosive chemicals are used in the Specialist section. Therefore, the use of an eyewash station is not necessary in the shop. In the event personnel are exposed to corrosives (fuel, hydraulic fluid, etc.) Nearest eye washing station is located within the Phase Bay area of the Maintenance Hangar along the east wall. Additionally,  there are additional eye washing stations located in the Phase back shop, along the north wall of the Maintenance Hangar, two stations in Fabrication back shop, and a eye wash/shower in the outside mech area adjacent the Haz Waste SAC. The path to the eye wash station needs to always be clear in case of an emergency. Be a good wingman. It’s everyone’s responsibility to take proper actions to assist personnel who are exposed and need to use the emergency shower and eyewash station, to include calling for medical assistance. 29 CFR § 1910.151(c) and 29 CFR § 1926.50(g), Medical Services and First Aid.
//User Guide: How to Use an Emergency Eye Wash Station: In an emergency scenario, an eyewash station can save your sight - if it’s properly used. Such accidents are fortunately very rare, but it’s paramount that you and your colleagues are prepared should the worst happen. 
1) Don’t delay. The moment a hazardous material enters your eyes, you should make your way to an eyewash station. Don’t hesitate, even if it’s only a minor spill - the longer a hazardous substance is in contact with the eye, the more damage it does. Even small amounts of contamination can cause serious injury and even permanent loss of vision.
2) Activate the unit. Push the activation lever on the eyewash station. When the lever has been pushed, the dust covers will pop open and each of the two eyewash nozzles will begin discharging water.
3) Flush out your eyes. Once activated, the eyewash station will continue to discharge water for a minimum of 15 minutes, meaning that it can be operated hands-free. Using your fingers to keep your eyelids open, lower your eyes into the stream of water issuing from the nozzles. Roll your eyes gently up and down and from side to side, ensuring that the water reaches as much of the eyeballs as possible.
4) Contact lenses. If you wear contacts, gently remove them once you have begun the flushing process. While failing to remove contact lenses can prevent the eye wash from properly irrigating the eyes, it is important not to delay flushing to take them out. Only do this once flushing has begun.
5) Keep on flushing. Continue to use the eyewash station in this manner for a full 15 minutes, and no less. This is the minimum amount of time that it takes to sufficiently clear the eyes of harmful chemicals - if you remove your eyes from the stream before this time has elapsed, you run the risk of permanent injury.
6) After flushing. When the 15-minute flushing period is over, seek medical assistance immediately. Have a colleague drive you to the accident and emergency department of your local hospital. Do not be tempted to drive yourself, as your vision may be impaired.
7) Shower Use . •In the event of an emergency, activate drench shower by pulling on pull rod. Begin to remove any clothing exposed to chemical or other hazardous substance (If eyes have been exposed to hazardous materials, follow procedure for eyewash use). •Flush eyes, face and body for 15 minutes. •After equipment use, seek a medical advisor immediately for further treatment.

meta.trafficSafetyNotes:
LOCAL TRAFFIC HAZARDS:  •	Poor road quality i.e., potholes, lose or uneven shoulders:  Be aware of surface conditions and take added caution in areas of road construction.  Move to the opposite lane when you encounter vehicles stopped on the side of the road i.e., Arizona State law requires the driver to move to the left lane when encountering an emergency vehicle on the right shoulder, if unable to move over then driver will slow down and move to the left most part of the lane, passing with extreme caution.
•	Weather conditions: Low lying roadways are prone to flooding and this area and subject to flash floods.  Slow down at night! With limited sight distance, comes limited reaction time.  Expect icy conditions on bridges, overpasses, and shaded areas during colder months when it rain, snow or freezes happen.  Dust storms do occur at times in Tucson and in between Tucson and Phoenix.  If you are caught in a dust storm and are able to pull to the side of the road turn off your lights, set park brake and keep foot off of brake.  If unable to pull off to the side of the road, reduce speed and proceed with caution.
•	Animal/Object Strikes: Coyotes and Javelina are mostly the largest animals you will encounter crossing roadways in the Tucson area.  In the outer parts of Tucson the roads go through open ranges which are where you may encounter a cow along the side of the road or in the road.  If you see a coyote or Javelina or other large animal, SLOW DOWN and attempt to drive by the animal in a controlled manner.  Attempting to steer around objects at high speed causes many other issues that can cause the driver to lose control i.e., running off the roadway, uncontrolled spin, roll over.

SPOTTERS:  Are required when operator visibility is obscured or in question, when backing a vehicle, and prior to beginning aircraft up/downloading (with pre-positioned chock in place).  Backing of government-owned motor vehicles and the usage of spotters will be IAW AFMAN 24-306. 
•	Spotter(s) will use a reflective belt and flashlight or luminous wand during hours of darkness or periods of reduced visibility: Reflective belt and flashlight or luminous wand.
•	Spotter(s) must be trained in standard hand and arm signals and flashlight signals before guiding a vehicle.
•	Spotter(s) will position themselves away from the vehicle's path of travel and maintain visual contact with the vehicle operator.
•	Government-owned motor vehicle operators will immediately stop if they lose visual contact with the spotter or notice the spotter is dangerously positioned between the vehicle and another object. In such cases, vehicle operators will secure the vehicle, exit and make an on-the-spot correction before continuing operations.

LICENSING/TRAINING REQUIREMENTS:  A state driver’s license is required to operate any vehicle. Additional training is dependent on duties/responsibilities.
•	Certificate of Competency required for all flightline driving and operation must be IAW AFI 13-213.
•	Before operating a Polaris Ranger/Razor, utility vehicle and other similar vehicles, personnel must complete LSV/OGMV training.

USE OF ELECTRONIC DEVICES:  Unless a hands-free device is used, use of cell phone is prohibited while operating a vehicle on base. Federal employees shall not engage in text messaging (a) when driving GMV, or when driving PMV while on official Government business, or (b) when using electronic equipment supplied by the Government while driving. Arizona law prohibits drivers from using a cellphone or a stand-alone electronic device while driving unless it is being used in a hands-free mode. This includes, but is not limited to, cell phones, tablets, and music & gaming devices.

selectedModules.title: Hazard Communication
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train personnel on hazardous chemicals in their work area, labeling systems, safety data sheets, and the measures they can take to protect themselves during normal operations and foreseeable emergencies.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Provide HazCom training upon initial assignment, whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced, and when new tasks expose workers to different hazardous materials. Ensure workers know how to access local SDS information and labeling guidance.
selectedModules.notes: Provide HazCom training upon initial assignment, whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced, and when new tasks expose workers to different hazardous materials. Ensure workers know how to access local SDS information and labeling guidance. Train personnel on hazardous chemicals in their work area, labeling systems, safety data sheets, and the measures they can take to protect themselves during normal operations and foreseeable emergencies. NOTE: The physical HAZCOM Program Binder is housed in the APG office (room 106). DAFI 90-821; 29 CFR 1910.1200 - Hazard Communication.

selectedModules.title: Hearing Conservation
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train noise-exposed employees annually on the effects of noise, the purpose of hearing protectors, the advantages and disadvantages of various protectors, and the purpose of audiometric testing.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Ensure workers enrolled in hearing conservation understand noise hazard areas, double-hearing protection requirements, and local follow-up actions tied to occupational health evaluations.
selectedModules.notes: The primary source of noise exposure to personnel above 92 dBA is active aircraft. BE has determined that engineering controls are not technologically feasible for this type of noise source. Consequently, personnel shall follow AFI 48-127_DAVISMONTHANAFBSUP for flightline hearing protection requirements, which may require the use of double hearing protection, and an octave band analysis is not required. Supervisors must conduct initial and annual workplace specific hearing conservation training for all personnel assigned and potentially exposed to hazardous noise. Additionally, personnel enrolled in the HCP must receive annual audiograms and training IAW OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95(k) and DAFI 48-127. Training slides can be obtained by calling 355 OMRS Public Health Flight at DSN: 228-2714. Training slides must be readily available, and annual training must be documented on the AF Form 55 or equivalent. DAFI 48-127; 29 CFR 1910.95 - Occupational noise exposure.

selectedModules.title: Bloodborne Pathogens
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Provide bloodborne pathogens training at initial assignment and at least annually thereafter, covering exposure control, modes of transmission, and protective measures.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Enroll applicable workers in the local bloodborne pathogens program and ensure exposure control plan requirements, reporting actions, and PPE procedures are covered before task performance.

selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Provide initial and task-specific explosives safety training using approved lesson plans, local instructions, and quantity-distance / compatibility controls before personnel work with explosives.

selectedModules.title: Electromagnetic Field Training

selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use approved EMF hazard assessments and local instructions to brief workers on hazard zones, signs, and restrictions before exposure.

selectedModules.title: Manual Lifting and Material Handling
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 20
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train workers on proper lifting techniques, team lifting, load assessment, and use of lifting aids to reduce musculoskeletal injury risk.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Provide verbal and written guidance on manual lifting, lifting devices, and local reporting actions for strain or overexertion symptoms.
selectedModules.trainingBasis: OSHA 2254 / Ergonomics and Material Handling Concepts
selectedModules.notes: Know your limitations. Supervisors shall ensure their workers receive thorough instruction and training on proper manual lifting techniques both routine or high risk and any PPE required. When a heavy object must be moved, get help or utilize mechanical equipment to move it. Supervisors shall instruct workers on their use. Also, proper lifting procedures must be used when moving any material. Proper lifting of heavy objects requires use of legs to lift the weight, not the back. Always use proper lifting techniques as learned in Manual Lifting training. Get help if you have any doubts about your ability to lift an object. Technicians are briefed annually through their work center JSTO which is documented on the member’s DAF 55. DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 20

selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use the JSTO and local fire prevention plan to brief workers on work-center fire hazards, alarm reporting, extinguisher use, and evacuation accountability.
selectedModules.notes:
Personnel are briefed on fire hazards, reporting procedures, extinguisher locations, evacuation routes, pull stations, and local emergency response actions annually through their work center JSTO which is documented on the member’s DAF 55.

selectedModules.title: Jewelry / Loose Articles Restrictions
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train workers on removing jewelry and securing loose articles when working around machinery, electrical hazards, rotating equipment, or snag hazards.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use local work-center restrictions and equipment guidance to define prohibited items and exceptions for mission-essential tasks.
selectedModules.notes: Maintenance Technicians must remove jewelry and secure loose articles when working around machinery, electrical hazards, rotating equipment, or snag hazards. During performance of duties in the office, wear of jewelry is not restricted. Jewelry will NOT be worn while conducting maintenance on the flight line, equipment and material handling, or other physical tasks. If there’s any doubt as to whether jewelry should be worn, remove it until you can get your supervisor’s approval. Technicians are briefed annually through their work center JSTO which is documented on the member’s DAF 55. DAFMAN 21-101 – Aircraft and Equipment Maintenance Management.

selectedModules.title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 14; 29 CFR Part 1910 - Occupational Safety and Health Standards (General Industry Standards) Subpart I; 29 CFR 1910.132; 29 CFR 1910.133; 29 CFR 1910.135; 29 CFR 1910.136; 29 CFR 1910.138
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train each affected worker on when PPE is necessary, what PPE is necessary, how to properly don, doff, adjust, and wear PPE, the limitations of assigned PPE, and the proper care, maintenance, useful life, and disposal of PPE. Require workers to demonstrate understanding and proper use before performing work requiring PPE, and retrain when workplace conditions, job assignments, PPE types, or worker knowledge gaps make prior training obsolete.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use the work-center JHA, BE occupational health assessment, manufacturer instructions, DAFMAN 91-203 Chapter 14, and local safety office guidance to identify PPE requirements. Supervisors must ensure PPE is provided, used, cleaned, inspected, maintained in sanitary and serviceable condition, and documented in JSTO training records. Cover eye and face protection, head protection, foot protection, hand protection, protective clothing, and respiratory or hearing protection when those programs apply.
selectedModules.notes:
The work-center JHA, BE occupational health assessment, manufacturer instructions, DAFMAN 91-203 Chapter 14, and local safety office guidance are used to identify PPE requirements. Supervisors will ensure PPE is provided, used, cleaned, inspected, and maintained in sanitary and serviceable condition. Technicians are briefed annually through their work center JSTO which is documented on the member’s DAF 55.
PPE is designed to protect the worker against biological, chemical, or physical hazards associated with the work environment. Normally, employees do not have a need for PPE in an office setting. However, there may be occasions when PPE may be necessary during some non-routine activities. Examples are moving furniture, painting or other minor cosmetic construction/facility up-keep, and other miscellaneous details. Before starting a task, consider what specific items and uses you may need PPE. 
• Foot Protection: Safety toe shoes - performing any maintenance and/or moving heavy equipment. 
• Arm/Hand Protection: Leather Safety Gloves - Pallet build-up/tear-down, moving heavy equipment, tying down heavy equipment for shipment, crating/uncrating equipment in wooden/fiberglass containers. 
• Nitrile, butyl, Chemical/Oil Resistant Gloves - Hazardous material or waste handling 
• Eye Protection: Face shield, safety glasses – soldering operations, compressed air/gasses, grinder/drill use, and safety wire operations, hammering, painting and using a punch or chisel, procedures involving Hydraulic Oil/Dielectric Coolant. Face shields will only be used as secondary eye and face protection in areas where splashing, rather than hazardous impact, is the problem. In the case of primary protection, other protective devices, such as safety goggles will be worn (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.133). 
• Hearing Protection: Ear plugs, ear defenders - Use as needed. We currently are not required to wear ear protection in the shop. However, both ear plugs and ear defenders are mandatory when performing maintenance on the flightline. • Other: Reflective Belts/Vests - Flightline maintenance during the hours of darkness, and during operation of bicycle/motorcycle. 
*NOTE: Personnel who wear contact lens or have medical conditions or take medications that may affect the use or wear of PPE must notify their supervisor immediately.
